MSK–SKIN · WEEK 16 · LECTURE 03

Inflammatory Arthritides

Colton Hoffer, MD · Learning-objective companion · Seronegative SpA, crystal-induced arthritis, imaging and targeted treatment

ObjectivesShared SpAMechanismAxial imagingSpA typesAutoimmunityCrystalsTreatmentReview

Learning objectives · source-based

  • Recognize shared features of seronegative spondyloarthropathies (SpA).
  • Contrast psoriatic, reactive, ankylosing, and IBD-associated SpA, including extra-skeletal findings.
  • Distinguish autoimmune from autoinflammatory mechanisms.
  • Compare gout and CPPD: presentation, mechanisms, diagnosis and treatment.

Exam priority: Dr. Hoffer marks certain slides with a gold border and stars (slides 8, 46, 47, 54, 66). These comparisons anchor the lecture.

Big picture: what is inflaming the joint?

Noninflammatory: osteoarthritis (covered in Lecture 2). Inflammatory: seronegative SpA, crystal-driven gout/CPPD, autoimmune arthritis, and infection-associated disease. A useful first decision is whether the clinical pattern is inflammatory axial disease, peripheral SpA, or a rapidly inflamed crystal joint.

MUST KNOW

Inflammatory back pain improves with movement and worsens with rest; mechanical pain usually has the reverse pattern.

Objective 1 · Shared seronegative SpA features

Seronegative refers to the absence of the typical known serum autoantibodies, not the absence of inflammation. Spondyloarthropathy is an overlapping family with axial sacroiliitis/spondylitis and/or peripheral enthesitis and arthritis.

PatternInflammatory low back painMechanical low back pain
OnsetInsidious; usually before age 45At any age; often more rapid
Morning stiffnessUsually >1 hourTypically ≤30 minutes
ExerciseImproves symptomsMay worsen symptoms
RestWorsens symptomsImproves symptoms
Nocturnal painFrequent; may wake from sleepTypically absent
Alternating buttock painCharacteristicTypically absent
NSAID responseOften goodVariable
ESR/CRPOften increasedUsually normal
  • Inflammatory low back pain: chronic morning pain/stiffness, improving with activity.
  • Peripheral arthritis: inflamed joints; often asymmetric in peripheral SpA.
  • Dactylitis: diffusely swollen “sausage” digit from joint synovitis plus flexor tenosynovitis.
  • Enthesitis: pain/inflammation where tendon, ligament, or capsule inserts into bone (Achilles and plantar fascia are classic).
  • Anterior uveitis: painful red eye with photophobia, ciliary flush; repeated disease can cause synechiae.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · A young adult’s back pain improves after walking at night and worsens after sitting: inflammatory or mechanical?

Inflammatory: prolonged morning stiffness, rest worsening, and relief with exercise fit axial SpA.

Why SpA creates both erosions AND new bone

The lecture models SpA as genetic predisposition (notably HLA-B27, plus many other loci) interacting with environmental triggers. The enthesis is an important initial inflammatory site. The course highlights the IL-23 → T-cell axis and TNF-α / IL-17 (synovium, skin, erosion) versus IL-22 (new bone formation).

MECHANISM

Enthesitis and osteitis → inflammatory erosion, while new bone formation across vertebral boundaries can lead to syndesmophytes and ankylosis. This helps explain why inflammation and apparent fusion coexist.

Objective 2 · Axial SpA and imaging patterns

Pattern 1: AS / nonradiographic axial SpA / IBD-associatedPattern 2: Psoriatic / reactive
Bilateral symmetric sacroiliitisOften asymmetric sacroiliitis
Ascending spinal involvement without skipsSpinal skip regions
Thin marginal syndesmophytes → bamboo spineBulky nonmarginal (“jug-handle”) syndesmophytes
EXAM TRAP

An early axial SpA patient can have an unrevealing radiograph; the lecture’s next test is STIR or T2 fat-suppressed MRI of the SI joints.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · How do thin continuous marginal syndesmophytes differ from jug-handle syndesmophytes?

Thin, marginal, continuous lesions point toward ankylosing/IBD-pattern axial disease; bulky nonmarginal asymmetric bridges and skips favor psoriatic or reactive SpA.

Objective 2 · Differentiate four SpA diagnoses

DiseaseDistinguishing cluesExtra-articular associations
Ankylosing spondylitisInflammatory axial pain, symmetric SI involvement, ascending marginal syndesmophytesAortitis/aortic regurgitation; costovertebral ankylosis restricting chest expansion; apical lung fibrosis
IBD-associated SpACrohn disease or ulcerative colitis; Type 1 peripheral asymmetric large-joint disease tracks IBD activity; Type 2 symmetric MCP polyarthritis does notErythema nodosum (tender red shin nodules); pyoderma gangrenosum (violaceous undermined ulcer)

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · What distinguishes Type 1 from Type 2 peripheral arthritis in IBD?

Type 1 = asymmetric large-joint oligoarthritis that follows bowel disease activity; Type 2 = symmetric small-joint polyarthritis, independent of bowel activity.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · A patient has lower-limb oligoarthritis after diarrhea plus conjunctivitis. What is the unifying diagnosis?

Reactive arthritis. Post-GI infection triggers a sterile joint inflammation; do not require all three classic triad elements.

Objective 3 · Autoimmunity versus autoinflammation

Autoimmune disease is driven by adaptive immunity and loss of tolerance involving autoantibodies or antigen-specific T cells. Autoinflammatory disease arises from dysregulated innate immunity, with stereotyped inflammatory episodes not explained by those adaptive responses.

COMMON CONFUSION

A disease can include both innate and adaptive immune components. The lecture places crystal arthritis (gout) toward the autoinflammatory end and rheumatoid arthritis toward autoimmunity.

Objective 4 · Crystal arthritis: distinguish gout from CPPD

GoutCPPD (“pseudogout”)
CrystalMonosodium urate: slender needlesCalcium pyrophosphate: rhomboid/rod
Polarized microscopyStrongly negative birefringenceWeakly positive birefringence
Typical acute site1st MTP (podagra) common; foot, knee and othersKnee and wrist; lecture states 1st MTP spared
AttackRapid-onset episodic asymmetric monoarthritisEpisodic monoarthritis; often slower onset than gout
ImagingTophi; punched-out “rat bite” erosions; ultrasound double contourChondrocalcinosis in cartilage/meniscus/TFCC

PreventionUrate lowering when indicated; goal serum urate <6 mg/dLNo crystal-removing treatment; treat associated metabolic disorder and prevent flares
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Which crystals and birefringence distinguish gout from CPPD?

Gout = monosodium urate needles, strongly negative; CPPD = rhomboids/rods, weakly positive.

Gout mechanism, triggers and treatment selection

Why urate accumulates: renal underexcretion is emphasized as the dominant pathway (~90%) versus overproduction (~10%). Hyperuricemia alone does not prove gout. Episodes may follow surgery, dehydration, renal decline, or diuretic use. The lecture lists purine metabolism defects (PRPP synthetase activation / HGPRT deficiency), high turnover and diet among overproduction factors.

  • Acute gout/CPPD flares: NSAIDs, glucocorticoids, colchicine; IL-1 receptor antagonist anakinra is included in this lecture.
  • Colchicine: disrupts microtubule assembly, impeding inflammasome function; its focus here is acute flare suppression/prophylaxis.
  • Chronic gout: urate-lowering therapy for recurrent flares, tophi, radiographic damage, or select high-risk first flares (CKD stage 3, serum urate >9 mg/dL, nephrolithiasis).
  • Allopurinol: lecture first-line urate-lowering agent when no contraindication; febuxostat is another xanthine oxidase inhibitor. Other named therapies include probenecid, pegloticase, and losartan.
  • Target: serum urate <6 mg/dL, with prophylaxis during urate mobilization. Do not treat isolated asymptomatic hyperuricemia under the lecture algorithm.
  • CPPD prevention: no agent removes CPPD crystals; consider colchicine prophylaxis for recurrent attacks and treat associated metabolic disease.
FIRST AID CONNECTION

Xanthine oxidase inhibitors reduce uric acid production, whereas uricosurics promote renal elimination. This mechanism-level contrast supports the lecture’s long-term gout therapy choices.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Why may a patient flare when beginning urate-lowering therapy?

Mobilization of established urate deposits can precipitate inflammation, so the lecture recommends temporary anti-inflammatory prophylaxis.

Master these before moving on

  • Inflammatory versus mechanical pain: the activity/rest relationship is a diagnostic branch point.
  • SpA imaging phenotype: symmetric thin continuous marginal bridges versus asymmetric skip lesions/nonmarginal bridges.
  • SpA extra-articular identifiers: bowel disease, infections, psoriasis/nails, aortitis, uveitis.
  • Innate versus adaptive: NLRP3–IL-1β crystal inflammation versus loss of self-tolerance.
  • Crystal identification: morphology, birefringence, joint preference, radiographic clues, acute versus preventive therapies.

The most useful First Aid connections

  • Urate lowering is a prevention strategy, not the immediate analgesic mechanism of acute gout treatment.
  • NLRP3-driven IL-1β release is a mechanistic bridge from deposited crystal to hot swollen joint.
  • “Bamboo spine” reflects ligamentous ossification and new bone, not cartilage loss alone.
Source: Colton Hoffer, MD, Inflammatory Arthritides, 67 slides; gold-border summaries are emphasized. First Aid / board enrichment is separately labeled.
